# SOPASair Walkthrough

This page describes the picoScan100 web interface and the settings in each view. Use it to commission the sensor before you automate the configuration through the API. To try the interface without a device, open it in the [Virtual Sensor Lab](../simulation/virtual-sensor-lab.md).

## Configuration

Choose the scan configuration and the core measurement behavior. Resolution, frequency, and range trade off against each other.

*Live capture from a picoScan100's web interface.*

The live scan on the left updates as you change the configuration, which is the quickest way to judge a setting.

### Basic Settings

Basic Settings controls the scan configuration used by the sensor. The settings
are shown on the right; the live scan on the left shows the effect of the
selected frequency, angular resolution, and other settings immediately. Use
this view to check coverage and measurement behavior while commissioning.

**Coordinate System**

The device coordinate system uses one point as the origin and reference for all
laser beams and distance measurements. With no translation into a world
coordinate system, this point is also the world origin.

The horizontal beam angle is **theta** (`θ`). A beam at `θ = 0°` points along
the middle of the sensor's main viewing direction, making the scan symmetric
around the X axis. The vertical elevation angle is **phi** (`φ`) and is
measured from the X/Y plane. For a single-plane picoScan, `φ = 0°` when the
sensor is ideally mounted.

<div>
<img src="../../assets/picoScan100/img/configuration-coordinate-system-xy.png" alt="Device coordinate system: theta" style="width: 220px; height: 220px; object-fit: contain;">
*Horizontal beam angle <strong>theta</strong>.*
</div>
<div>
<img src="../../assets/picoScan100/img/configuration-coordinate-system-xz.png" alt="Device coordinate system: phi" style="width: 220px; height: 220px; object-fit: contain;">
*Vertical beam angle <strong>phi</strong>.*
</div>

Measurement data is always output in the device coordinate system. Transform it
into a world or application frame on the receiving system after accounting for
the sensor's mounting position and orientation. See
[3D point clouds with 2D LiDARs](../integration-notes/3d-with-2d-lidars.md) for an
example coordinate transform.

**Date and system time**

The time base can be set using various methods:

- Explicitly setting the date and time
- Transferring the time from the computer used
- Via an external NTP server (Network Time Protocol) that is accessible in the network. The technology uses UDP on port 123. This setting is recommended to ensure a correct time stamp in the detection history or error entries.
- Via an external PTP (Precision Time Protocol) master that is accessible in the network. The technology uses UDP on ports 319 and 320. This setting is recommended for precise synchronization requirements (e.g. between several devices).

**Dynamic Sensing Profiles**

LiDAR applications often need different sensor characteristics at different
times. An AMR may need the shortest response time in busy areas, a large
scanning range and good angular resolution in a warehouse, and the highest
close-range angular resolution while docking. Higher angular resolution
requires a lower scanning frequency, so choose the priority for each
application.

Dynamic Sensing Profiles allow the scan's core parameters to be changed during
operation without restarting the sensor. The Scan Data Configuration function
allows fast switching between profiles:

<p class="table-caption" markdown>**Basic Settings:** profile, frequency, angular resolution, and typical use.</p>

| Profile | Frequency | Angular resolution | Typical use |
| ---: | ---: | ---: | --- |
| 1 | 15 Hz | 0.5° | Object detection with large scanning ranges |
| 2 | 15 Hz | 0.33° | TiM series retrofit |
| 3 | 20 Hz | 0.1° | Fine positioning or environment maps |
| 4 | 20 Hz | 0.25° | Low-noise measurements; recommended for LiDAR-LOC |
| 5 | 25 Hz | 0.25° | LMS100 series retrofit |
| 6 | 30 Hz | 0.1° | Fine positioning or environment maps |
| 7 | 40 Hz | 0.25° | Fast object detection at a large scanning range |
| 8 | 50 Hz | 0.25° | Very fast object detection |
| 9 | 15 Hz | 0.05° | Highest angular resolution for static measurements |
| 10 | 40 Hz | 0.125° | High angular resolution and high scan rate |
| 11 | 15 Hz | 1° | TiM series retrofit |

Available profiles depend on the device variant and license; see
[Licenses](./licenses.md).

### Filter

Clean up the scan before it leaves the sensor by suppressing extra echoes, artifacts and airborne particles.

![Filter settings](../assets/picoScan100/img/configuration_filter_tile_20260826_153236.png)
*Example filter settings in the picoScan100 web interface. Select parameters according to the requirements of each application.*

If present, the filters are applied in the following order:

1. Fog filter
2. Echo filter
3. Particle filter
4. Moving average filter
5. Filters for data reduction and the region of interest filter

For detailed behavior and examples, see [Filter details](../data-streaming/filter-details.md).

### Inertial Measuring Unit (IMU)

Use the IMU view to inspect the sensor's current orientation and acceleration.

*Live capture from a picoScan100's web interface.*

The IMU view displays the yaw, pitch, and roll angles in degrees, together with the measured acceleration on the X, Y, and Z axes in meters per second squared. The orientation indicator provides a visual representation of the current sensor position.

Use these values as a guide when checking the sensor installation or interpreting the scan coordinate system.

### Contamination Indication

Monitor the optics cover for dirt and get a warning before measurement quality drops.

*Live capture from a picoScan100's web interface.*

The contamination status provides a live reading of Clean, Minor, Heavy, or Blocked. The segment wheel identifies where contamination is accumulating around the optics cover. Configure whether contamination triggers a warning, an error, or both, and adjust the sensitivity and outputs for the environment.

### Connection Options

Give the sensor its permanent Ethernet identity so it fits your network.

*Live capture from a picoScan100's web interface.*

Choose static addressing to enter a fixed IP address, or DHCP to have a server assign the address automatically, according to your application and network requirements. The IP address must be unique on your network. The subnet mask defines which addresses are local, for example `255.255.255.0`, and the default gateway provides access to other subnets. The MAC address and calculated speed are read-only values for reference and firewall rules.

1. Set the addressing mode to Static.
2. Enter the IP, subnet mask, and gateway for your network.
3. Press Apply.
4. Reconnect the browser at the new address.

Pressing Apply drops your current browser connection.

### Inputs and Outputs

Configure the multifunction I/O ports and map field-evaluation results and device states to physical outputs.

*Live capture from a picoScan100's web interface.*

Set each port as an input or an output and give it a name.
Bind an output to a source, such as a field-evaluation result or a device state.
Configure the logic (HIGH or LOW active), inversion, restart behavior, and status log.
The right panel shows the live status and counters for every port.

I/O is a simple way to connect a PLC when you do not want to parse the data stream.

### Field Evaluation

Draw 2D detection fields and let the sensor decide, on the device, when something enters them.

*Live capture from a picoScan100's web interface.*

Fields are 2D zones that you draw around the sensor in its scan plane. The sensor reports a detection when points fall inside a field. Evaluation groups combine fields with logic and produce an actionable result. A field state can drive a physical output (see [Inputs and outputs](#inputs-and-outputs)) or appear in the detection list for your software. A group can remain active continuously or be switched by an input, for example to monitor a zone only while a machine is moving. Pan and zoom the scan view to check field coverage across the full aperture angle.

Because the evaluation runs on the sensor, this detection works without an external computer.

The following capture shows how to add a detection field in the web UI. Every field lives inside an evaluation group that pairs the field geometry with the logic and output reacting to it.

*Live capture of creating a detection field on a picoScan100.*

1. On the Field evaluation panel, click **Add group** to create an evaluation group.
2. The group opens an evaluation chain: Field → Evaluation → Output.
3. Click the Field node to define the field geometry: draw a contour, or use Teach-in to capture the current environment as the field.
4. Set the evaluation logic and wire the result to an output; the field then appears live in the 2D view.
5. Click the floppy-disk icon in the toolbar to save the configuration permanently (until you do, changes live in RAM and are lost on restart).

New evaluation groups can only be *created* in the web UI or by restoring a configuration that already contains them. Once they exist, the [REST API](../configuration/rest-interface.md) can modify their contours and activate them at runtime.

### Perpendicular Distance Measurement

Measure the perpendicular distance from the sensor's scan line to the nearest
object inside a zone, and stream that distance as a live result.

*Live capture from a picoScan100's web interface.*

*This video shows how to receive measurement data via CoLa.*

Like [field evaluation](#field-evaluation), detection runs on the device inside evaluation groups, but the result is a distance value rather than a simple field-clear/field-infringed state.

Each group holds a Perpendicular distance measurement evaluation that reports how far the closest object is, measured perpendicular to the scan.
Read the live values from the Result list for distance measurement, or over the [REST API](../configuration/rest-interface.md) / [WebSocket events](../data-streaming/websocket-events.md).
Object detection tuning keeps the reading stable. The Max. blanking size setting ignores gaps smaller than the set width, and the Detection time setting sets how long an object must be present (in scans) before it counts.

1. On the Perpendicular distance measurement panel, click **Add group**.
2. Draw the zone the measurement applies to, the same way you draw a field.
3. Set Max. blanking size and Detection time under Object detection to
   match your target and required responsiveness.
4. Read the distance in the Result list for distance measurement, or wire it
   into your software over the API.
5. Click the floppy-disk icon to save the configuration permanently (until you do,
   changes live in RAM and are lost on restart).

Because the measurement runs on the sensor, you get a ready-to-use distance value without processing the raw scan on a host.

![Result list for distance measurement](../assets/picoScan100/img/application_perpendicular_distance_result_list.png)
*The Result list shows the minimum and maximum distance and the coordinates of the measuring points for each evaluation.*

# Asset Administration Shell

The Asset Administration Shell (AAS) is the standardized digital twin of Industry 4.0. SICK publishes an AAS for each product part number at [aas.sick.com](https://aas.sick.com). Access requires a SICK ID login. The AAS describes the product type in a machine-readable format, which makes it useful for engineering tools and asset management systems.

## What to Expect

- **Nameplate:** manufacturer, product designation, order code, and markings such as CE and UKCA
- **Technical data:** product classification (ECLASS, ETIM) and key technical properties
- **Documents:** data sheet, operating instructions, dimensional drawing, and certificates
- **CAD data:** 3D models such as STEP files and the EPLAN macro
- **Contact information:** SICK sales and service contacts

The AAS describes the part number, not an individual device. Serial number, firmware version, configuration, status, and measurement data come from the device itself through the [REST API](../configuration/rest-interface.md), the [CoLa interface](../configuration/cola-interface.md), and the data streams.

## Link a Device to Its AAS

Each device is identified by its product ID
[`pid.sick.com/{P/N}/{S/N}`](https://pid.sick.com/), made of the part number
and the serial number from the type label. Both values can also be read from
the device over the REST API. The part number connects the device to its AAS.

# Checksums

The `LFTchecksum` is a read-only REST resource that returns MD5 digests over four independent software and configuration areas of the device. It lets you verify at any time that nothing has changed since a known-good reference: detect unintended parameter changes, confirm a configuration file applied correctly, or check that a firmware update touched only the areas it should.

## Reading It

No authentication required:

```http
GET /api/LFTchecksum
```

```json
{
  "header": { "status": 0, "message": "Ok" },
  "data": { "LFTchecksum": {
    "MD5SumOK":       true,
    "MD5LinuxRoot":   "8439a3f5bb209f3d51557d509169ec60",
    "MD5App":         "304f9a18302e2b635da2c2c220463119",
    "MD5Calibration": "bc5e5d5df638dc45c85937c8c67b59d7",
    "MD5Parameters":  "07f18c8032e24ac65ca0ed7c04be6a62"
  } }
}
```

## The Four Sub-Checksums

<p class="table-caption" markdown>**The Four Sub-Checksums:** field, covers, and changes when….</p>

| Field            | Covers                            | Changes when…                                                                          |
| ---------------- | --------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `MD5LinuxRoot`   | Linux root filesystem (OS layer)  | A firmware update modifies the OS partition                                            |
| `MD5App`         | Application binary and libraries  | A firmware update installs a new application version                                   |
| `MD5Calibration` | Factory calibration data          | Calibration is recalculated/overwritten (factory service only)                         |
| `MD5Parameters`  | Persistent parameter set (EEPROM) | Parameters are persisted via `WriteEeprom`, or a config file is imported and persisted |
| `MD5SumOK`       | Overall integrity flag            | `false` if any of the four fails its internal verification                             |

## RAM vs. Persistent Storage

The device keeps two parameter states at once:

<p class="table-caption" markdown>**RAM vs. Persistent Storage:** parameter state, storage location, persistence after reboot, and effect on `MD5Parameters`.</p>

| State          | Where          | Survives reboot?                                                                    | Reflected in `MD5Parameters`?             |
| -------------- | -------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------- |
| Working copy   | RAM            | No (a `RebootDevice` flushes RAM to EEPROM first, so it survives a software reboot) | No, until `WriteEeprom` or `RebootDevice` |
| Persisted copy | EEPROM / flash | Yes                                                                                 | Yes                                       |

Every REST write modifies only the RAM copy. `MD5Parameters` (the persisted digest) does not change until `WriteEeprom` is called, or the device is rebooted via `RebootDevice` (which persists RAM first). A `SoftReset` or a hard power-cycle discards unsaved RAM changes.

After a REST write, reading an unchanged `MD5Parameters` means the change is still in RAM only, not that the device is unmodified. Persist with `WriteEeprom` (or reboot) to make the change durable and visible in the checksum.

## When Does Each Sub-Checksum Change?

The following table shows the behavior of a picoScan150 (● = changed, - = unchanged):

<p class="table-caption" markdown>**When Does Each Sub-Checksum Change?** Scenario and resulting change of the LinuxRoot, app, calibration, and parameters checksums.</p>

| Scenario | LinuxRoot | App | Calibration | Parameters |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Two consecutive reads, no operation | - | - | - | - |
| Change a parameter in RAM only (no `WriteEeprom`) | - | - | - | - |
| Change in RAM, then `SoftReset` | - | - | - | - |
| Change in RAM, then `RebootDevice` (persists first) | - | - | - | ● |
| Change + `WriteEeprom` | - | - | - | ● |
| `CreateParameterBackup` → `RestoreParameterBackup`, same file, no content change | - | - | - | - |
| `LoadApplicationDefaults` (destructive) | - | - | - | ● |
| Firmware upgrade | ● | ● | - | - |
| Firmware downgrade | ● | ● | - | - |

`MD5Calibration` does not change through normal end-user operations. A change there indicates a factory calibration update or an unexpected write to the calibration partition, so treat it as a red flag.

## A Practical Integrity Workflow

1. Record all four hashes from a known-good device (the reference).
2. After any change (a config push, a [restore](../configuration/configuration-backup-and-restore.md), a [firmware update](./firmware-update.md)), read `LFTchecksum` again.
3. Compare field by field: a firmware update should move `MD5LinuxRoot` + `MD5App` only; a persisted config change should move `MD5Parameters` only; `MD5Calibration` should never move.
4. Anything else is unexpected: investigate before putting the device back into service.

Compact and MSGPACK telegrams carry a CRC32 per packet (see [Compact Format](../data-streaming/compact-format.md#frame-layout)); CoLa B telegrams carry a 1-byte XOR checksum. The `LFTchecksum` covers the stored software and configuration, which complements these on-the-wire checks.

# Device Discovery

This page explains the available discovery methods for locating a SICK LiDAR sensor on the network. Use the method that best fits your commissioning environment to find the device address quickly.

There are three ways to find a sensor:

1. [Use the default IP](#default-ip) for a direct first connection.
2. [Use SOPAS ET network search](#sopas-et-network-search) when the sensor is already connected to a local network.
3. [Implement discovery yourself](#your-own-implementation) when discovery must be part of an application or provisioning workflow.

## Default IP

For a direct first connection, connect the sensor to the computer with Ethernet and use the factory default IP address:

<p class="table-caption" markdown>**Default IP:** parameter and value.</p>

| Parameter | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Sensor IP address | `192.168.0.1` |
| Subnet mask | `255.255.255.0` |

Set the computer's Ethernet adapter to a different address in the same subnet, for example `192.168.0.100`, then open `http://192.168.0.1/` in a browser. See [Getting started](../getting-started.md) for the Windows procedure.

## SOPAS ET Network Search

SOPAS ET provides a graphical network search for SICK devices. Connect the sensor to the same Ethernet segment as the computer and start the search. The result lists responsive devices with their IP address, MAC address, and device identity.

![SOPAS ET device search](../assets/shared-features/sopas-et-device-search.png)
*SOPAS ET network search showing a discovered picoScan device.*

Use this approach when the sensor is already connected to a switch or when its configured address is unknown. The search uses the same local broadcast principle as the protocol described below; it does not cross routers.

## Your Own Implementation

SICK devices answer a UDP broadcast discovery telegram, so a host on the same segment can locate every device without knowing its address in advance. This requires no authentication and no REST call: send one broadcast datagram to `255.255.255.255:30718`; every responsive device replies by unicast with its full network configuration.

This is a limited broadcast: it travels only within the local segment and is discarded at every router boundary. If the device is on a different subnet, connect a host to the same segment and set the address explicitly.

### Finding an Address When Discovery Is Disabled

The picoScan100 can disable SICK's proprietary UDP-broadcast discovery for cybersecurity reasons. When disabled, it does not reply to the standard search in SOPAS ET or SICK AppManager, but it still announces its address through standard network mechanisms such as Gratuitous ARP.

Connect the sensor to your computer or a local network switch, capture packets on the relevant Ethernet interface in Wireshark, and apply the display filter:

```text
arp
```

Locate an entry whose MAC address begins with `00:06:77`, the SICK device prefix, and read its IP address from the ARP packet details.

On Windows, run `arp -a` from an elevated Command Prompt and locate an address whose MAC begins with `00-06-77`. On Linux, run `arp -n` and locate a MAC beginning with `00:06:77`. The corresponding IP address belongs to the sensor. These commands work only when the sensor is in the current subnet; to locate a sensor outside the default subnet, configure the network adapter with a wider subnet mask such as `255.0.0.0`.

### Request Telegram (24 Bytes)

Each field is at a fixed position:

<p class="table-caption" markdown>**Request Telegram (24 Bytes):** bytes, field, value / source, and description.</p>

| Bytes | Field        | Value / source      | Description                                                                |
| ----- | ------------ | ------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| 0     | CMD          | `0x10`              | Command identifier for a scan (discovery) request                          |
| 1     | isBC         | `0x00`              | Unicast/broadcast origin flag, set `0x00` even when broadcasting           |
| 2-3   | Length       | `0x00 0x08`         | Payload length, big-endian; always 8 for discovery                         |
| 4-9   | Host MAC     | `FF:FF:FF:FF:FF:FF` | Sender MAC; all-ones for a broadcast request                               |
| 10-13 | Request ID   | random 4 bytes      | Fresh random per telegram; devices echo it so you can match replies        |
| 14    | Scan flag    | `0x01`              | Marks a scan request; the device ignores the telegram if this isn't `0x01` |
| 15    | Reserved     | `0x00`              | Must be zero                                                               |
| 16-19 | Interface IP | host address        | Host interface IPv4, one byte per octet (big-endian)                       |
| 20-23 | Subnet mask  | host mask           | Host subnet mask, one byte per octet (big-endian)                          |

### Sending the Broadcast

```python
sock = UDP_socket()
sock.set_option(SO_BROADCAST, 1)
sock.set_option(SO_RCVTIMEO, 5)
sock.bind(interface_ip, port=0)
```

```python
requestID = random_bytes(4)
telegram = build_telegram(interface_ip, subnet_mask, requestID)
sock.sendto(telegram, dest="255.255.255.255", port=30718)
```

```python
while True:
    data, sender = sock.recvfrom(1024)
    if timeout:
        break
    device = parse_response(data)
    print(device)
```

```python
sock.close()
```

Do **not** stop after the first reply: keep receiving until the 5 s timeout expires so you collect every device.

### Parsing the Replies

Each reply is a variable-length packet whose configuration fields are tagged: a 4-byte ASCII tag, a 2-byte internal header, then the field bytes. To extract a field, find its tag, skip 2 bytes, read the defined number of bytes:

```python
index = buffer.find(tag)      # 4-byte ASCII tag
start = index + 4 + 2         # skip tag (4) + internal header (2)
value = buffer[start : start + field_length]
```

<p class="table-caption" markdown>**Parsing the Replies:** tag, field, size, and encoding.</p>

| Tag    | Field             | Size | Encoding                       |
| ------ | ----------------- | ---- | ------------------------------ |
| `EIPa` | Device IP address | 4    | IPv4 big-endian                |
| `ENMa` | Subnet mask       | 4    | IPv4 big-endian                |
| `EDGa` | Default gateway   | 4    | IPv4 big-endian                |
| `EDhc` | DHCP flag         | 1    | `0x01` = DHCP, `0x00` = static |
| `EMAC` | MAC address       | 6    | hex bytes, MSB-first           |

If a tag isn't found, that field isn't present in the response.

### Platform Notes

Set `SO_BROADCAST` before sending, or the send fails. On a multi-homed host, bind the socket to the IP of the adapter on the device subnet so the broadcast leaves the correct network interface card. On Windows, set the sensor network profile to Private; a Public profile blocks the inbound unicast replies. See [Getting started](../getting-started.md).

SICK's discovery tools perform the same broadcast with a GUI. Use them for a quick look; use the raw telegram above when you need discovery built into your own application or a headless provisioning script.

# Firmware Update

The available update methods depend on the product family and firmware.
multiScan100 firmware can be updated through SOPAS ET, Sentio Creator, the web
UI (SOPASair), or supported REST endpoints. LRS4000 firmware can be updated
through SOPAS ET or SICK AppManager. Check the product-specific release notes
before updating.

## Where to Get the Package

Download the package that matches your device and target version from the device's product page on [sick.com](https://www.sick.com) under *Downloads* / *Software*.

- [picoScan100](https://www.sick.com/de/en/catalog/products/lidar-and-radar-sensors/lidar-sensors/picoscan100/pics150-01000-pro-1/p/p677850?category=g569793&tab=downloads)
- [multiScan100](https://www.sick.com/de/en/catalog/products/lidar-and-radar-sensors/lidar-sensors/multiscan100/muls1aa-114322-multiscan165/p/p680210?category=g568283&tab=downloads)
- [multiScan200](https://www.sick.com/de/en/search?text=multiScan200)
- [LRS4000](https://www.sick.com/de/en/catalog/products/lidar-and-radar-sensors/lidar-sensors/lrs4000/c/g555594?tab=downloads)

For multiScan100, multiScan200, and picoScan100, [Sentio Creator](../visualization/sentio-creator.md), which can also provide firmware packages as well.

Read the release notes for your device before you update:
[LRS4000](../LRS4000/release-notes.md),
[multiScan100](../multiScan100/release-notes.md),
[multiScan200](../multiScan200/release-notes.md), or
[picoScan100](../picoScan100/release-notes.md).

## Web GUI

Open the device's firmware page in SOPASair and follow the update workflow.

![Firmware update in the Web GUI](../assets/shared-features/firmware-update-webgui.png)
*Firmware update in the Web GUI.*

## Sentio Creator

Use Sentio Creator to discover the device, select the firmware version, and install the update.

![Firmware update in Sentio Creator](../assets/shared-features/firmware-update-sentio-creator.png)
*Firmware update in Sentio Creator.*

## Headless via the REST API

Automate the update with the five steps below. Run them in order; skipping or reordering steps can leave the device in an inconsistent state. After flashing, the device reboots automatically and is unreachable for a few minutes. The update is successful only when the device is back online with the expected version.

### Get a Session Token

multiScan200 and picoScan100 use `POST /api/CreateSessionToken` at Service
level with [challenge-response](../configuration/rest-interface.md#challenge-response-authentication)
in the JSON body. This endpoint also accepts HTTP Basic authentication, which
is convenient in scripts:

```http
POST /api/CreateSessionToken
Authorization: Basic <base64(Service:<password>)>
Content-Type: application/json

{}
```

Basic authentication sends the password only Base64-encoded. Use it only over HTTPS or on an isolated network.

The response contains the session token:

```json
{ "header": { "status": 0 }, "data": { "token": "eyJhbGci..." } }
```

The multiScan100 REST interface documents `/update`, `RunFirmwareUpdate`, and
`UpdateState`, but not `CreateSessionToken`. Use the authentication flow from
the release notes or the OpenAPI file for the installed firmware.

### Upload the Package

`PUT /api/update` with the firmware file as the binary body. On multiScan200
and picoScan100, the `X-Session-Token` header authorizes this transfer, so
Basic Auth is not required here.

```http
PUT /api/update
X-Session-Token: <token>
Content-Type: application/octet-stream

<binary firmware file content>
```

A `200 OK` confirms the package was received.

### Start the Update

`RunFirmwareUpdate` is a protected method requiring [challenge-response](../configuration/rest-interface.md#challenge-response-authentication) in the JSON body. Basic Auth and the session token are not accepted here, so fetch a fresh challenge immediately before calling it.

```http
POST /api/RunFirmwareUpdate
Content-Type: application/json
```

Fetch a fresh challenge and compute the hash for `POST:RunFirmwareUpdate`, then send it in the JSON body:

```json
{
  "header": {
    "nonce": "...",
    "opaque": "...",
    "realm": "...",
    "user": "Service",
    "response": "<computed hash>"
  }
}
```

### Poll the Update State

`GET /api/UpdateState` every ~5 s until it reaches Finished (2) or the device becomes unreachable (reboot started). Stop on Error (3) and investigate before retrying.

```http
GET /api/UpdateState
```

Example response:

```json
{ "data": { "UpdateState": 1 } }
```

### Verify the New Version

After the device is back online, read the identity and compare against the expected version:

```http
GET /api/DeviceIdent
```

Example response:

```json
{ "data": { "DeviceIdent": { "Name": "picoScan", "Version": "2.3.3.0R" } } }
```

`DeviceIdent.Version` and `GET /api/FirmwareVersion` may format the same firmware version slightly differently, so normalize them before comparing.

## UpdateState Values

<p class="table-caption" markdown>**UpdateState Values:** value, state, and meaning.</p>

| Value | State    | Meaning                                                                                |
| ----- | -------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| 0     | Initial  | No update in progress. Package may be uploaded but flashing hasn't started.            |
| 1     | Started  | Flashing in progress. Do not power-cycle the device.                                   |
| 2     | Finished | Flash complete; the device reboots automatically.                                      |
| 3     | Error    | Update failed. Check package compatibility and retry. Do not power-cycle immediately.  |

## Error Handling

- `PUT /api/update` returns 403: Missing or expired session token. Create a fresh token and add `X-Session-Token`.
- `RunFirmwareUpdate` returns `header.status` 4 (Access Denied) or 10 (Invalid Challenge): Basic Auth or the session token was used instead of challenge-response, or the challenge was invalidated. Use a new [challenge](../configuration/rest-interface.md#challenge-response-authentication) for `POST:RunFirmwareUpdate`.
- `UpdateState` = 3 (Error): Wrong package or an unsigned package on firmware V2.2.0 or later. Download the correct `.spk.signed` and retry.
- Device never returns: Normal reboot takes 2-5 minutes. Wait and keep UDP sockets open across the reboot.

While `UpdateState` is Started (1), never power-cycle the device. Allow 2-5 minutes total for the flash and reboot. Keep measurement sockets open across the reboot, so the OS doesn't buffer an ICMP port-unreachable message that would break the first `recv()` call afterwards (on Windows, apply `SIO_UDP_CONNRESET`).

On picoScan100, subscribe to the [`UpdateState` WebSocket event](../data-streaming/websocket-events.md) instead of polling to get progress pushes during the flash. On multiScan200 and picoScan100, verify integrity after the update with the [`LFTchecksum`](./checksums.md): a firmware change updates `MD5LinuxRoot` and `MD5App` but leaves `MD5Parameters` and `MD5Calibration` untouched.

# LiDAR License Management

Some device functions require a license. Use the device's license manager to
transfer an issued license code to the device. The exact screens and available
options can vary by device and firmware.

## Before You Begin

- Obtain a valid license code for the device. The code is formatted as five
  groups separated by hyphens.
- Connect to the device and open its web interface.

## Activate a License

1. In a browser, connect to the device at
   `http://<device-IP-address>/`. On the device overview, choose **View licenses**.

   ![Device overview with the View licenses link highlighted.](../assets/shared-features/license-manager-device-overview.png)
   *Open the license overview from the device home page.*

2. In the license overview, choose **Activate license**.

   ![License overview showing available licenses and the Activate license and Deactivate license actions.](../assets/shared-features/license-manager-license-list.png)
   *The license overview also provides the action to deactivate returnable licenses.*

3. Select whether the device has an internet connection for the transfer, then
   choose **Next**.

   ![License Manager asks whether an internet connection is available for license activation.](../assets/shared-features/license-manager-transfer-connection.png)
   *Choose the transfer route that matches the device's network access.*

4. Enter or copy the license code. If the license ticket contains several
   entries, select the license entries to transfer, then continue.

   ![License ticket selection screen with selectable entries and group licenses option.](../assets/shared-features/license-manager-select-licenses.png)
   *Select the entries that should be transferred to the device.*

5. When the transfer succeeds, close the confirmation and check the updated
   license overview.

6. Reboot the device.

## Deactivate or Return a License

In the license overview, choose **Deactivate license**. During license
selection, enter the license code for the license to deactivate,
choose a license marked as returnable, then continue and confirm.

# Time Synchronization

This page describes how to synchronize sensor clocks with NTP or other time sources. Accurate timestamps help you align measurements from multiple sensors and correlate scans with external system events.

## NTP Time Synchronization

NTP synchronizes the sensor clock with an NTP server on the network. Use it when timestamps must match a common time base across systems, such as recorded sensor data, logs, or external applications.

An Ubuntu host on the sensor network can provide a shared clock without Internet access. Install and start the NTP service to set up an offline Ubuntu NTP server:

```bash
sudo apt update
sudo apt install ntp
sudo systemctl enable --now ntp
```

Configure `/etc/ntp.conf` to use the host's local clock and accept local queries:

```ini
server 127.127.1.0 prefer
fudge 127.127.1.0 stratum 10
restrict 127.0.0.1
restrict ::1
```

Restart the service after changing the configuration:

```bash
sudo systemctl restart ntp
```

To configure the sensor as an NTP client in SOPASair, open **Configuration → Basic settings → Date and system time**, choose the time zone and update rate, and enter the Ubuntu host's IP address. Save the settings and allow time for the next configured update. The sensor status page shows when synchronization completes.

![Date and system time configuration tile](../assets/picoScan100/img/configuration_date_and_system_time_tile_20260826_153228.png)
*Date and system time tile in SOPASair.*

Through the REST API, set `TSCRole` to `1` for NTP client mode and set `TSCTCSrvAddr` to the server address. `TSCRole` accepts `0` (no time synchronization), `1` (NTP client), and `3` (PTP slave); other values are rejected with `header.status` 9 (Illegal Value). The sensor cannot act as an NTP server. `LSPdatetime` reads the current sensor time and `LSPsetdatetime` sets it manually.

To verify connectivity, check the service and local time on Ubuntu with `sudo systemctl status ntp` and `timedatectl`. Test the server with `ntpdate -q 127.0.0.1`, inspect NTP packets with `sudo tcpdump -i any udp port 123 -v`, and permit NTP through UFW with `sudo ufw allow 123/udp` when UFW is enabled.

Ensure that the sensor can reach the selected NTP server through the configured network and firewall. See [REST API / OpenAPI](../configuration/rest-interface.md) for parameter access.

## PTP Time Synchronization

PTP synchronizes the sensor clock with other devices on a local network using the Precision Time Protocol. Use it for high-precision timestamp alignment when data from multiple sensors or other time-sensitive systems must be fused.

![Date and system time settings with PTP selected](../assets/shared-features/ptp-date-and-system-time.png)
*Date and system time settings with PTP selected.*

### Sensor Settings

The sensor uses fixed IEEE 1588 PTPv2 End-to-End (E2E) settings. It operates as an ordinary clock receiving synchronization from a master. Step mode is detected automatically: software PTP uses one-step operation and hardware PTP uses two-step operation. Its `clockClass` is `255`, indicating slave-only operation.

### Master Configuration

Configure the PTP grandmaster with settings compatible with the sensor:

<p class="table-caption" markdown>**Master Configuration:** parameter and required value.</p>

| Parameter | Required value |
| --- | --- |
| PTP profile | IEEE 1588 PTPv2 E2E |
| Transport protocol | UDPv4 |
| `logAnnounceInterval` | `1` (2 seconds) |
| `logSyncInterval` | `0` (1 second) |
| `announceReceiptTimeout` | `3` |
| `logMinDelayReqInterval` | `0` (1 second) |
| Domain number | `0` |

Enable PTP in the sensor time-synchronization settings, or set `TSCRole` to `3` through the REST API, then connect it to this compatible PTP grandmaster. All participating devices must use the same domain, and network infrastructure must forward PTP traffic correctly.

With native ROS 2 on multiScan200 and picoScan100, the device publishes its
hardware PTP timestamp in each message header. See [Native ROS 2](../integration-notes/ros-integration.md#native-ros-2)
for the available topics.

# User Levels

User levels control who can change the sensor configuration. Reading live data and status does not require a login, but configuration changes, methods, and protected API requests do.

<p class="table-caption" markdown>**User Levels:** user level and factory state on multiScan200 and picoScan100.</p>

| User level | Factory state on multiScan200 and picoScan100 |
| --- | --- |
| Service | Enabled |
| Maintenance | Disabled |
| Authorized Client | Disabled |

For multiScan200 and picoScan100, only Service is enabled in the documented
factory state. Check the product documentation for the multiScan100 or
LRS4000 variant to confirm its factory state. On devices where the other
levels are disabled, a Service-level user must enable them before they can be
selected. Activate only the levels required by the deployment, then assign
and protect their passwords before handing the system over.

## Enabling a User Level

Log in to SOPASair with the Service user level, open the user-level management settings, enable the required level, and set its password. Save the configuration permanently with Write EEPROM so the setting persists after a power cycle.

![User levels and access data tile](../assets/picoScan100/img/diagnosis_cyber_security_access_data_tile_20260826_153405.png)
*Access this tile in SOPASair via **Diagnostic → Cybersecurity**.*

REST API clients enable or disable REST user levels with `EnableUserLevel`. In the challenge-response `header.user` field, write the levels as `Service`, `Maintenance`, and `AuthorizedClient`. CoLa A/B clients use `EnableLegacyUserLevel` for their respective user levels. Authenticate these changes as Service, and use a fresh [challenge-response](../configuration/rest-interface.md#challenge-response-authentication) value for each protected REST request.

See [REST API / OpenAPI](../configuration/rest-interface.md) for REST authentication and [Challenge Response Authentication](../configuration/rest-interface.md#challenge-response-authentication) for the request flow.

## Resetting the Password

1. Establish a connection to the product in the web browser.
2. Select **Log In**.
3. Select **Password forgotten?**.
4. Send the device key, serial number, and part number by email to the responsible SICK sales company or the responsible SICK service partner, see [sick.com/worldwide](https://www.sick.com/worldwide).
5. Click **Next** to confirm.
   - The window for entering a code appears. You can get the code from the responsible SICK sales company or the responsible SICK service partner. The code is only valid once for the reset process. You can close the window by clicking on the x without interrupting the reset process. If you select **Cancel** or enter an incorrect code several times, the current reset process is terminated. The requested code is no longer valid. The process must be restarted.
6. Optional: close the window. At a later time, open the window for entering the code via **Settings** and **Password forgotten?**.
7. Enter the code.
8. Click **Reset** to confirm.
   - The password is reset to the default password. Parameters are not changed.

<!-- Source: https://sickag.github.io/sick_lidar_developer_guide/integration-notes/3d-with-2d-lidars/ -->

# 3D with 2D LiDARs

The picoScan100 measures distance and intensity in a single plane. Mounting it on a motorized axis (tilt, rotation, or a linear stage) sweeps that plane through 3D space. If an incremental encoder is attached to the axis, the rotation angle at the moment of each scan is known precisely. This means every 2D point can be rotated into a common 3D frame, and a full sweep becomes a dense 3D point cloud.

Two approaches exist. Choose based on where you want the geometry code to run.

<p class="table-caption" markdown>**3D with 2D LiDARs:** comparison criterion, Approach A (host-side), and Approach B (on-device).</p>

|              | Approach A (host-side)                                      | Approach B (on-device)                             |
| ------------ | ----------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------- |
| Angle source | Encoder wired to the sensor                                 | Encoder wired to the sensor, or the built-in IMU   |
| Processing   | Host receives raw UDP frames and applies the 3D transform   | Device accumulates and saves a PCD file internally |
| Result       | One host-generated `.pcd` per sweep                         | Single `.pcd` from `GET /cloud.pcd`                |
| Best for     | Custom transforms, real-time streaming, maximum flexibility | Simple integration, no host-side geometry code     |

For every scan frame, the sensor sends an encoder telegram (Compact type 4) with the same `frame_number` and the encoder tick count. This gives frame-accurate synchronization without timing jitter between the scan and position streams. Encoder input is available on the picoScan150.

## Hardware and Ports

A typical example is a sensor on a motorized tilt axis with a SICK DFS60-series incremental encoder wired to the sensor's encoder input. The same idea applies to rotation or linear stages: what matters is that an encoder on the moving axis feeds the sensor so each scan frame carries a position value.

<p class="table-caption" markdown>**Hardware and Ports:** stream, protocol, port, and content.</p>

| Stream       | Protocol    | Port | Content                                                       |
| ------------ | ----------- | ---- | ------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Scan data    | Compact UDP | 2115 | 2D distance + intensity per segment, with `frame_number`      |
| Encoder data | Compact UDP | 7504 | `tick_count`, reference ticks, speed, `frame_number`          |

Enable encoder data output (`EncoderDataEnable`, destination in `EncoderDataEthSettings`, default port 7504) and reset the encoder counter at the reference position before you collect data. The [Configuration backup & restore](../configuration/configuration-backup-and-restore.md) flow is a convenient way to apply a validated encoder configuration.

## Approach A: Host-Side Transform

### Synchronize by Frame Number

Both UDP streams carry a `frame_number`. Build a lookup table from that number to the encoder tick, so you can retrieve the exact axis angle for any scan frame even when the two streams arrive slightly out of order:

```txt
on encoder packet:  encoder_map[packet.frame_number] = packet.tick_count
on scan frame:      tick = encoder_map.lookup(frame.frame_number)  # or most-recent tick
```

Keep the table bounded in size to avoid unbounded memory growth over long acquisitions.

### Coordinate Transform

Convert each encoder tick to an angle, then rotate the 2D scan point around the axis. For a tilt axis along the world Y-axis with the scan plane horizontal at the reference:

```txt
theta   = (tick / ticks_per_revolution) * 2 * PI      # radians
x_world = x_scan * cos(theta)
y_world = y_scan                                       # lateral axis unchanged
z_world = x_scan * sin(theta)
```

Set ticks-per-revolution correctly. This value is specific to your encoder model. A mismatch produces a distorted point cloud. Reset the encoder counter at the reference position so tick 0 is your angular origin, and adapt the transform for a different axis orientation or a linear stage.

### End-to-End Pseudocode

Reset the encoder counter to establish tick 0:

```http
POST /api/mResetEncoderIncrement
```

Process the two UDP streams and transform each scan frame:

```python
encoder_map = {}          # frame_number -> tick
cloud_pts   = []

def on_encoder_packet(pkt):
    encoder_map[pkt.frame_number] = pkt.tick_count

def on_scan_frame(frame, points_2d):
    tick  = encoder_map.get(frame.frame_number, last_known_tick)
    theta = (tick / TICKS_PER_REV) * 2 * PI
    for (x, y, intensity) in points_2d:
        cloud_pts.append({ x: x*cos(theta), y: y, z: x*sin(theta), intensity })

udp_listen(port=2115, callback=on_scan_frame)
udp_listen(port=7504, callback=on_encoder_packet)
run_until_interrupted()
save_pcd(cloud_pts, "cloud.pcd")
```

The [sick_perception_sdk](programming-tools-and-examples.md) (C++17) is a good starting point for a host-side implementation.

## Approach B: On-Device Scan Merger

The on-device scan merger runs entirely on the device. While the sensor rotates, it combines consecutive 2D profiles into a 3D point cloud and saves a `.pcd` file in device storage. The host only needs to trigger, poll, and download the result with one HTTP GET; no UDP parsing or transform code is required. The angle source is configurable (encoder, or the built-in IMU when no encoder is available).

![3D scan recording interface](../assets/picoScan100/img/application_pointcloud_20260826_153132.png)
*Live capture of the 3D scan recording interface on a picoScan100.*

### Configuration Parameters

<p class="table-caption" markdown>**Configuration Parameters:** parameter, endpoint, values, and description.</p>

| Parameter           | Endpoint                      | Values                    | Description                          |
| ------------------- | ----------------------------- | ------------------------- | ------------------------------------ |
| `ScanMergerEnabled` | `POST /api/ScanMergerEnabled` | `true` / `false`          | Enable the scan merger               |
| `ScanMergerSource`  | `POST /api/ScanMergerSource`  | `0` (IMU) / `1` (ENCODER) | Rotation reference                   |
| `ScanMergeTrigger`  | `POST /api/ScanMergeTrigger`  | `0` (METHOD)              | Start/stop via method calls          |
| `RotationOffset`    | `POST /api/RotationOffset`    | `{x, y, z}` in mm         | Sensor offset from the rotation axis |

Setting parameters and calling merger methods requires [challenge-response authentication](../configuration/rest-interface.md#challenge-response-authentication).

### Workflow

1. Configure the merger parameters and persist them with `WriteEeprom`.
2. `POST /api/ResetScanMergeView`: clear any previous recording.
3. `POST /api/StartScanMerge`: start recording while the axis moves.
4. `POST /api/StopScanMerge`: stop recording after the sweep.
5. Poll `GET /api/MergeSaving` until it changes from `true` (saving) back to `false`. The point cloud is then ready.
6. `GET /cloud.pcd` (port 80, outside `/api/`): download the point cloud, for example `curl http://192.168.0.1/cloud.pcd -o cloud.pcd`.

Only the most recent point cloud is available. The scan merger is a one-shot recorder: it accumulates on the device and stores one PCD file. There is no continuous 3D output. For continuous 3D, use Approach A or the [Compact stream](../data-streaming/compact-format.md) with your own accumulation.

# Cybersecurity

Download the product-specific Cybersecurity Hardening Guide from **Downloads**
on the individual product page at [sick.com](https://www.sick.com/):
[LRS4000](https://www.sick.com/de/en/search?text=LRS4000),
[multiScan100](https://www.sick.com/de/en/search?text=multiScan100),
[multiScan200](https://www.sick.com/de/en/search?text=multiScan200), or
[picoScan100](https://www.sick.com/de/en/search?text=picoScan100).

Cybersecurity covers the entire product life cycle. Increasing digitalization and
network complexity in production plants increases the risk of cyberattacks from
inside or outside the production network. A comprehensive cybersecurity strategy
is therefore essential.

The asset owner is responsible for installing and maintaining security measures.
Securing SICK devices in a network requires the active participation of the
asset owner.

The recommendations below apply to the LRS4000, multiScan100, multiScan200,
and picoScan100. Menus, default states, available services, and authentication
requirements vary by family, variant, and firmware. Sections with device-specific
values name the products they cover. Confirm settings in the product-specific
hardening guide and the device interface before applying them.

This page covers:

- Communication security and access management
- Application and field-evaluation aspects
- User levels
- Device interfaces
- Ethernet-related settings

## Further Cybersecurity Information

For a cybersecurity overview, see [SICK PSIRT](https://www.sick.com/psirt).
Current security advisories are listed on the
[SICK PSIRT Security Advisories](https://www.sick.com/de/de/product-security-incident-response-team-psirt/security-advisories/s/psirt-advisories)
page. Report security issues to the SICK
Product Security Incident Response Team (SICK PSIRT). Read SICK's Information
Handling Policies before sending security details.

Product-specific settings and telegram details are available from the device
documentation. The product page is available through the SICK Product ID:
[`pid.sick.com/{P/N}/{S/N}`](https://pid.sick.com/), where `{P/N}` is the part
number and `{S/N}` is the serial number shown on the type label. The same part
number links the
device to its [Asset Administration Shell](../shared-features/asset-administration-shell.md),
which holds the data sheet, operating instructions, certificates, and CAD data
of the product type.

The examples and recommended settings on this page are general guidance, not
customer-specific solutions or a replacement for specialist technical advice.
Use the product-specific hardening guide and product documentation for the
device and firmware in your installation.

## General Recommendations

### Intended Use

These are non-contact LiDAR sensors for indoor or outdoor, mobile or stationary
use in stand-alone operation. LRS4000 and picoScan100 are 2D LiDAR families;
multiScan100 and multiScan200 are multi-layer 3D LiDAR families. Depending on
the device, configuration, and application software, typical applications
include:

- Continuous output of measurement data
- Monitoring freely defined fields, with object detection signaled through
  digital outputs or telegrams
- Stationary field protection, area monitoring, and access control
- Navigation and anti-collision for mobile platforms
- Profile detection, collision protection, object protection, and access
  monitoring
- 3D mapping, environment perception, and volume monitoring (multiScan200)

Use the device only in industrial environments (EN 61000-6-4). Incorrect use,
improper modification, or tampering invalidates any warranty and may result in
damage for which SICK AG accepts no responsibility.

### Environmental Influences

For outdoor variants, fog, steam, dust, rain, and snow can affect the detection
range. The effect can only be quantified through a verification test at the
intended site.

### Restrict Physical Access

Operate the device in a protected area where only instructed and approved
personnel have access.

### Limit Exposure to Public Networks

Do not use the devices in public networks. Use an isolated
network wherever possible to reduce exposure and risk.

### Establish an Update Strategy

Keep the device firmware up to date:

1. Search for the product at [sick.com](https://www.sick.com).
2. Check **Downloads** for the latest firmware version and release notes.
3. Check for updates regularly and apply them as they become available.
4. Test updates in the specific installation before deploying them at larger
   scale.

Perform firmware updates only in a trusted environment. Release notes contain
information about included security patches.

### Configuration Backup and Restore

Keep a protected backup of a known-working configuration so that the device
can be returned to a secure state. The
[Backup & restore](../configuration/configuration-backup-and-restore.md)
workflow supports multiScan100, multiScan200, and picoScan100. A passphrase can
encrypt the backup. File-transfer authentication differs by firmware; follow
the instructions for the matching OpenAPI file.

### Data Integrity

Verify downloaded `.spk` and `.sdd` files with the instructions at
[sick.com/verify-downloads](https://www.sick.com/verify-downloads). The
[`LFTchecksum` workflow](../shared-features/checksums.md) is available on
multiScan200 and picoScan100.

### Brute-Force Protection

After five consecutive unsuccessful login attempts, the picoScan100 enters a
30-second time lock. Do not assume the same threshold or lockout duration on
other families; check their product-specific hardening guide.

### Periodic Security Tests

Regularly verify that the security system works as intended and document the
results.

### Device Identification

Verify that the correct device type and system plug are connected. The product
ID uniquely identifies the device and consists of its part number and serial
number. Find the product ID on the device and system-plug labels, or read it
through the user interface.

The device information also shows the currently installed firmware version,
which follows semantic versioning. The device part number can also be read
through the API:

```http
GET http://192.168.0.1/api/OrderNumber
```

Read the serial number with `GET http://192.168.0.1/api/SerialNumber`. Together
they form the product ID
[`pid.sick.com/{P/N}/{S/N}`](https://pid.sick.com/). See
[Link A Device To Its AAS](../shared-features/asset-administration-shell.md#link-a-device-to-its-aas)
to connect this ID with the product type data.

For telegram-based access, refer to the [CoLa / LMDscandata](../data-streaming/lmdscandata-format.md)
documentation and the [Compact format](../data-streaming/compact-format.md).

### Use the Device-Not-Ready Status

The Device-Not-Ready status signals that the device is not operating correctly.
Monitor it through communication or a digital output. A change to this state
while device parameters are being changed can be used as a manipulation
warning.

## Protection Levels

Each protection level assumes that the recommendations from the previous level
are followed.

<p class="table-caption" markdown>**Protection Levels:** protection level, intended use, and procedures.</p>

| Protection level | Use for | Procedures |
| --- | --- | --- |
| No protection | Demonstrations or test scenarios | Set factory defaults |
| Basic protection | Recommended minimum for daily operation in an uncritical environment | Check firmware and release notes; change all passwords; configure network settings; disconnect unused interfaces; close unused ports and services |
| Advanced protection | Exposed or critical systems with advanced security requirements | Apply basic protection and limit network access by IP range |

### No Protection

In this state there are no access restrictions: passwords remain at their
defaults and interfaces are active. Do not use this state for daily operation.
Use it only for demonstrations or tests, or when physical access is restricted
and the device is isolated from the network or protected by a firewall.

#### Set Factory Defaults

To start from a known state:

1. Log in to the device with user level **Service**.
2. Verify the user level.
3. Set the device to factory defaults.

The device resets default passwords and reboots with the standard IP address
`192.168.0.1`. If a different IP address was previously used, either open the
default address in a web browser or search for and reconnect to the device in
SOPAS ET.

### Basic Protection

Basic protection is the minimum recommended level for daily operation in an
uncritical environment.

#### Check Firmware and Release Notes

Critical vulnerabilities can be discovered during the device life cycle.
Updating firmware is therefore an important cybersecurity measure. Before
commissioning, install the latest firmware and review its release notes for
security patches. Update only in a trusted environment.

#### Change Passwords

Enable only the user levels required by the deployment and assign each a unique,
secret password. Factory user-level states vary by family and firmware. Follow
the [User levels](../shared-features/user-levels.md) guide for the current
activation and password workflow.

Use passwords containing uppercase letters, lowercase letters, special
characters, and numbers. Change passwords over a confidential connection,
preferably a point-to-point connection during initial commissioning.

#### Reset the Service Password (picoScan100)

<div class="device-scope" data-device-scope="picoScan100" markdown="1">

On picoScan100, only the Service password can be reset to its default through
the password-reset process:

1. Select **Password forgotten**.
2. Send the generated email to the responsible SICK sales company or service
   partner listed at [sick.com/worldwide](https://www.sick.com/worldwide).
3. Paste the received code and select **Reset**.

Selecting **Cancel** aborts the process. Request a new reset code from the
manufacturer if necessary.

To regain access to another user level, first reset the Service password, back
up the configuration, and then reset the device to factory defaults.

</div>

#### Configure Network Settings

The documented factory network defaults for the device families covered here
are:

<p class="table-caption" markdown>**Configure Network Settings:** setting and default.</p>

| Setting | Default |
| --- | --- |
| IP address | `192.168.0.1` |
| Subnet mask | `255.255.255.0` |
| Default gateway | `0.0.0.0` |

<div class="device-scope" data-device-scope="multiScan200 picoScan100" markdown="1">

The following network-service defaults are for multiScan200 and picoScan100
only:

<p class="table-caption" markdown>**Configure Network Settings:** service, port, multiScan200, and picoScan100.</p>

| Service | Port | multiScan200 | picoScan100 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| HTTP (web server, REST) | TCP `80` | Enabled | Enabled |
| CoLa A / CoLa B | TCP `2111` / `2112` | Disabled | Enabled |
| CoLa2 | TCP `2122` | Disabled | Always enabled |
| Device search | UDP `30718` | Enabled | Time-limited |

</div>

LRS4000 and multiScan100 also provide a **Diagnostics > Cybersecurity** view
with service and protocol information. Check that view on the target device;
do not infer their defaults from the table above. The
[LRS4000](../LRS4000/graphical-user-interface.md#cybersecurity) and
[multiScan100](../multiScan100/graphical-user-interface.md#cybersecurity)
walkthroughs show where to inspect these settings.

#### Disconnect Unused Interfaces

If a communication interface is not used by the application, disconnect its
communication cable. For example, an application using only digital I/O does
not need a permanently connected communication interface used only for
parameterization.

#### Close Unused Ports and Services

Disable every protocol that is not required for operation. This reduces the
device's attack surface.

##### Legacy Protocols (CoLa)

CoLa1 (CoLa ASCII/Binary) is a legacy interface for configuration and status
requests. Disable it when the application does not need it. On multiScan200
and picoScan100, manage this service under **Diagnostics > Cybersecurity**;
CoLa1 is disabled by default on multiScan200 and enabled by default on
picoScan100. On LRS4000 and multiScan100, inspect the service state and
available controls on the device before changing it.

##### SOPAS ET Device Search

Limit device visibility through broadcast scanning. On picoScan100, the device
search setting offers four modes:

<div class="device-scope" data-device-scope="picoScan100" markdown="1">

<p class="table-caption" markdown>**SOPAS ET Device Search:** mode and behavior.</p>

| Mode | Behavior |
| --- | --- |
| Enabled | The device can be discovered and its IP address can be changed without authentication. |
| Time-Limited | The device can be discovered and its IP address can be changed without authentication for 60 seconds after boot. |
| Restricted | The device can be discovered, but its IP address cannot be edited without authentication. |
| Disabled | The device cannot be discovered. **Recommended where applicable.** |

Device search uses UDP port `30718`. It is **Time-Limited** by default on the
picoScan100.

</div>

<div class="device-scope" data-device-scope="multiScan200" markdown="1">

On the multiScan200, device search is enabled by default; disable it in
**Diagnostics > Cybersecurity** when it is not required.

</div>

On LRS4000 and multiScan100, check the device's cybersecurity service list for
the device-search service and its current state. The picoScan100 modes and
default values above do not necessarily apply to those families.

##### Web Server

<div class="device-scope" data-device-scope="multiScan200 picoScan100" markdown="1">

On multiScan200 and picoScan100, the web server uses TCP port `80` and is
enabled by default. It provides browser-based visualization and
parameterization; when disabled, the sensor remains reachable through SOPAS
ET. For LRS4000 and multiScan100, inspect the cybersecurity service list and
the product-specific hardening guide before disabling web access.

</div>

##### CoLa2

<div class="device-scope" data-device-scope="multiScan200 picoScan100" markdown="1">

CoLa2 uses TCP port `2122`. On picoScan100 it cannot be disabled. On
multiScan200 it is disabled by default; enable it in
**Diagnostics > Cybersecurity** only when required. Check the product-specific
service list for CoLa2 availability on other families.

</div>

##### Measurement Data Output

Enable measurement data output only when required:

1. Log in as **Authorized client**.
2. Open **Application > Data output > Measurement data output**.
3. Enable UDP streaming.

Enabling measurement data output opens a device-side UDP port. Disabling it
closes that port again.

##### IMU Data Output

Where supported by the device variant and licenses, configure IMU output under
**Application > Data output > IMU data output** as **Authorized client**.
Enable UDP streaming only when required. It opens a device-side UDP port;
disabling the stream closes the port.

##### Digital I/O

Configure digital signals for device-specific application signals, such as
DeviceNotReady or field evaluations, under **Configuration > Inputs and
outputs**. Log in as **Authorized client**.

##### Date and System Time

Configure synchronized time under **Basic settings > Date and system time**
as **Authorized client**, where this setting is available. NTP uses network
time-server traffic. All four families support PTP over UDP ports `319` and
`320`. Check the device's service list and
[time-synchronization guide](../shared-features/time-synchronization.md) for
supported methods and current state.

##### User Levels

<div class="device-scope" data-device-scope="multiScan200 picoScan100" markdown="1">

On multiScan200 and picoScan100, only **Service** is enabled in the documented
factory state; it cannot be deactivated. Factory user-level states can differ
on LRS4000 and multiScan100. Check the
[User Levels](../shared-features/user-levels.md) guide and the product-specific
hardening guide before enabling or disabling a level.

</div>

#### Use Encrypted Communication

Use HTTPS to encrypt web-interface and REST communication. Measurement data
sent over UDP or TCP is not encrypted by HTTPS. Follow the
[HTTPS & certificates](../configuration/https-and-certificates.md) guide to upload a valid
certificate bundle and verify the enabled state.

### Advanced Protection

Advanced settings are applied in addition to the basic settings.

#### Limit Network Access by IP Range

Change the default IP address to a non-default value and limit the subnet mask
to the smallest subnet that meets the application's needs. Subnetting reduces
broadcast traffic and makes it easier to isolate network problems.

Configure this under **Configuration > Connection options > Ethernet** as
**Service**.

## Application-Related Recommendations

### Primary Sensor Data

The supported data formats vary by family. Use the
[Data Streaming overview](../data-streaming/index.md) to choose a format
available on the device and review its security implications. Measurement
data sent over UDP or TCP is not encrypted by HTTPS. The notes below on
telegram fields are limited to the named formats and families.

#### Compact Format (Recommended)

Compact packets contain user data and a CRC32 checksum. Telegram headers and
fields differ by format and family.

<div class="device-scope" data-device-scope="LRS4000 multiScan100 picoScan100" markdown="1">

Type 1 scan telegrams are used by LRS4000, multiScan100, and picoScan100.

</div>

<div class="device-scope" data-device-scope="multiScan200" markdown="1">

multiScan200 uses type 6 scan telegrams.

</div>

Consult the [Compact format guide](../data-streaming/compact-format.md) for the
device-specific fields used to check data identity, ordering, timing, and
integrity.

#### MSGPACK Format (multiScan100 and picoScan100)

<div class="device-scope" data-device-scope="multiScan100 picoScan100" markdown="1">

MSGPACK is available on multiScan100 and picoScan100. The following packet
fields and segment details describe the documented picoScan100 structure;
check the matching product documentation before relying on them for another
family.

</div>

<div class="device-scope" data-device-scope="picoScan100" markdown="1">

<p class="table-caption" markdown>**MSGPACK Format (multiScan100 and picoScan100):** field and purpose.</p>

| Field | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| Telegram counter | Counts measurement-data telegrams since power-up, starting at `1`; detects lost data. |
| Transmit timestamp | Sensor system time in microseconds since 1970-01-01 00:00 UTC; detects delays. Synchronize the sensor with a time server where required. |
| Segment counter | Identifies segments. A 276° frame is split into 10 segments of 30° or 5 segments of 60°, depending on the scanning frequency. |
| Frame number | Counts frames since device startup; detects lost data. |
| Sender ID | Contains the device serial number; identifies the sending sensor. |
| CRC32 checksum | Follows the user data and is calculated over the MSGPACK buffer only, without the STX bytes and the size field. |

</div>

#### LMDscandata Format (LRS4000, multiScan100, and picoScan100)

<div class="device-scope" data-device-scope="LRS4000 multiScan100 picoScan100" markdown="1">

LMDscandata is available on LRS4000, multiScan100, and picoScan100. The
following field details describe the documented picoScan100 structure; check
the product-specific telegram listing for another family:

</div>

<div class="device-scope" data-device-scope="picoScan100" markdown="1">

<p class="table-caption" markdown>**LMDscandata Format (LRS4000, multiScan100, and picoScan100):** field and purpose.</p>

| Field | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| Serial number | Identifies the sending device. |
| Telegram counter | Counts telegrams created since power-up, starting at `1`; detects lost data. |
| Version number | Identifies the serialization version and helps trace structure changes. |
| Scan counter | Counts scans actually created by the device. |
| Time since startup | Counts microseconds since power-up, starting at `0`. |
| Device time | Sensor system time since 1970-01-01 00:00 UTC in microseconds; detects delays. |
| XOR checksum | Verifies transfer integrity. CoLa B only: one byte, the XOR of all data bytes. |

</div>

### Secondary Sensor Data

multiScan100 and picoScan100 use Compact type `2` for IMU data.
multiScan200 uses type `7`, with its standard header. The LRS4000 provides
IMU data through CoLa events or the REST API instead of Compact. Use the
[Compact format guide](../data-streaming/compact-format.md#type-2-imu) for
device-specific IMU fields:

- Telegram version: the described telegram structure uses version `1`.
- IMU sensor timestamp: sensor system time in µs since 1970-01-01 00:00 UTC;
  detects delays in the data stream.
- CRC32 checksum: CRC32 of all words except the checksum.

### Device State

Monitor device state to detect changes in parameterization:

- CoLa `sRN SCdevicestate` transmits the general device state.
- REST `GET /api/DeviceStatus` reads the device status.

### Recommended Security Measures

#### Last Modified Information

Protect and monitor the information about when device parameters were changed
and stored. Find it under **Diagnosis > Overview > Operating information**.

#### Messages

Regularly review the diagnostic overview under **Diagnosis > Overview >
Messages**. If the sensor is not working as intended, use the troubleshooting
information to correct the problem or determine how to proceed.

#### Diagnostic File

The device provides a diagnostic file for in-depth analysis. Only SICK can read
this file. Use NTP synchronization so that device information can be assigned
correctly:

1. Log in as **Service**.
2. Open **Basic settings > Date and system time** and configure NTP or PTP.
3. Open **Diagnostics > Overview > Diagnostic file**.
4. Select **Create file**, then download the file.

#### Changing Parameters

Prevent unauthorized operators from changing parameters because parameter
changes can alter application results. Limit access to device parameters to the
minimum number of people required by the need-to-know principle.

# MATLAB Integration

MATLAB ROS Toolbox can subscribe directly to native ROS 2 data from
multiScan200 or picoScan100 through DDS. No SICK ROS driver or bridge is
required. The example below uses picoScan100 point-cloud data on
`/cloud/all_points` as `sensor_msgs/PointCloud2` with the default ROS domain
ID `0`.

## Validated Setup

<p class="table-caption" markdown>**Validated Setup:** component and version or setting.</p>

| Component | Version / setting |
| --- | --- |
| Operating system | Windows 11 |
| MATLAB | R2025b with ROS Toolbox |
| ROS 2 / DDS | Kilted with CycloneDDS |
| ROS domain ID | `0` (device default) |

All DDS participants must use the same domain ID as the sensor. Ensure that the sensor's native ROS 2 interface is enabled and that the computer firewall allows DDS traffic. See [Native ROS 2](ros-integration.md#native-ros-2) for sensor-side setup.

## Receive PointCloud2 Data

The following script creates a MATLAB ROS 2 node, lists visible topics, and prints the number of points received on `/cloud/all_points`.

```matlab
node = ros2node("/matlab_cloud_counter");

disp("Available ROS 2 topics:");
disp(ros2("topic", "list"));

sub = ros2subscriber( ...
    node, ...
    "/cloud/all_points", ...
    "sensor_msgs/PointCloud2", ...
    @onPointCloud);

disp("Subscribed to /cloud/all_points");

t0 = tic;
while toc(t0) < 10
    pause(0.1);
end

clear sub node
disp("Finished.");

function onPointCloud(msg)
    pointCount = double(msg.width) * double(msg.height);
    fprintf("PointCloud received: %d points\n", pointCount);
end
```

## Visualize Live Data

Open **Apps** > **ROS 2 Data Analyzer**, choose **Open** > **Live Network Data**, select **Live ROS 2 network data**, and set the ROS domain ID to `0`. Create a PointCloud Visualizer, choose `/cloud/all_points`, then select **Start**.

## Verify Connectivity

Use the ROS 2 CLI independently of MATLAB to verify that DDS data is present:

```sh
ros2 topic echo /cloud/all_points
```

If no data is visible, confirm the native ROS 2 interface configuration,
firewall rules, DDS compatibility, and ROS domain ID. On multiScan200 and on
picoScan100 from firmware V2.3.1, the sensor domain ID is configurable
(`rosDomainId`); make sure MATLAB uses the same value.

# Model Context

When developing an application for a SICK LiDAR sensor, you can clone the
relevant documentation or code repository into your project workspace. A local
copy gives your coding assistant access to the repository's examples,
configuration files, API usage, and implementation details while you work.

Clone the
[SICK LiDAR Developer Guide](https://github.com/SICKAG/sick_lidar_developer_guide)
repository alongside your application:

```sh
git clone https://github.com/SICKAG/sick_lidar_developer_guide.git
```

Keep the clone up-to-date when you need the latest context:

```sh
git -C sick_lidar_developer_guide pull
```

This repository-based approach provides source context for your development
tools. It is **not an MCP server** and does not expose an MCP tool or service.
